monitor.tuningPresetsHelpPre: Pick the result you want — each is a short, by-hand checklist of guided steps. The steps adapt to your graphics card by name
monitor.tuningPresetsHelpPost: . Advisory only: Compy never changes these for you; it just shows the way.

visual-fidelity.label: Max Quality
visual-fidelity.goal: Make games look their best — richer color and a tear-free picture.

smooth.label: More FPS
smooth.goal: Chase higher, steadier frames — full RAM speed, Game Mode, a tear-free sync.

clarity.label: Lower Latency
clarity.goal: A more responsive PC — free up drive headroom, prioritize the game, and cut background drag.

cpuTempOffer.title: Turn CPU temperature on
cpuTempOffer.why: Compy ships no driver of its own — that is what keeps it anti-cheat-safe — so it shows the temperature a free monitor app publishes.
cpuTempOffer.publishingWithoutCpuTemp: {{app}} is publishing sensors, but no CPU temperature among them. In {{app}}, check that the CPU package sensor (Tctl/Tdie) is switched on.
cpuTempOffer.sharedMemoryOff: HWiNFO is running, but its Shared Memory Support is off — that switch is what lets Compy read the temperature.
cpuTempOffer.sharedMemoryHow: In HWiNFO: Settings → tick “Shared Memory Support” → OK. The free version turns it back off roughly every 12 hours.
cpuTempOffer.notPublishing: {{app}} is running but isn’t publishing sensors. It has to be started as administrator before it can read them.
cpuTempOffer.installedNotRunning: You already have {{app}} — start it and the temperature shows up here.
cpuTempOffer.startHwinfoNote: HWiNFO asks Windows for administrator rights itself — that prompt is HWiNFO’s, not Compy’s.
cpuTempOffer.starting: Starting {{app}} — this panel checks again on its own for the next few seconds.
cpuTempOffer.startFailed: Compy couldn’t start {{app}}. Open it from your Start menu and the temperature shows up here.
cpuTempOffer.installTitle: Install either one and Compy reads the temperature from it. Nothing to set up in Compy.
cpuTempOffer.hwinfoNote: Gamer-trusted. After installing, switch on Shared Memory Support (Settings → Shared Memory Support).
cpuTempOffer.lhmNote: Open-source, no time limit. Heads-up: its low-level driver can trip strict anti-cheat (Valorant/Vanguard) — close it before those games.

sessionDebrief.leftOut: {{span}} left out while another window was in front.
sessionDebrief.screenTarget: Your average was about {{pct}}% of your {{rate}} Hz screen.
sessionDebrief.screenTargetMet: Your average kept up with your {{rate}} Hz screen.
sessionDebrief.noChangeSub: The difference is smaller than this rig's own session-to-session noise. Claiming a win here would be lying.
sessionDebrief.improvedSub: Measured on this rig, in {{game}}, above its own noise across these two sessions — a real signal, not a guarantee for every game or session. You applied it; Compy measured it.
sessionDebrief.regressedSubPost: in {{game}}. No spin — take it back.
sessionDebrief.confoundedSub: Other changes landed between these two sessions — this delta can't be honestly attributed to {{title}}. No credit either way.
sessionDebrief.expiredSub: This was armed too long ago to compare fairly — drivers, games, and Windows move on. Re-arm fresh from a new debrief.
sessionDebrief.unmeasuredNoiseSub: Compy hasn't measured how much {{game}} moves between your sessions with nothing changed, so it won't call this better or worse. A few more sessions of {{game}} with nothing changed let the next comparison be judged.
sessionDebrief.unmeasuredCapSub: The frame cap wasn't the same in both {{game}} sessions, or Compy couldn't read it, so this comparison can't be judged.
sessionDebrief.unmeasuredConditionsSub: Compy couldn't confirm the two {{game}} sessions were played under comparable conditions (for example, a different GPU), so this comparison can't be judged.
sessionDebrief.unmeasuredDeltaLine: Average {{avgSign}} FPS ({{avgPct}}%), worst-moment FPS (1% low) {{lowSign}} FPS ({{lowPct}}%), not judged.
sessionDebrief.deltaLineMeasured: Average {{avgSign}} FPS ({{avgPct}}%), worst-moment FPS (1% low) {{lowSign}} FPS ({{lowPct}}%) - {{inOut}} the +{{rise}}% / -{{fall}}% this game moves between your sessions with nothing changed
sessionDebrief.deltaLine: Δ average {{avgSign}} FPS ({{avgPct}}%) · worst-moment FPS (1% low) {{lowSign}} FPS ({{lowPct}}%) — {{inOut}} the ±{{noiseFloor}}% normal run-to-run wobble (the noise floor)
sessionDebrief.noChangeMeansPre: That's a real answer, not a failure — a lesser tool would have called this a win. One suspect cleared:
sessionDebrief.noChangeMeansPost: It didn't help this game; it may still help heavier ones. Keep it or take it back — one click either way.

background.headline: Not graded
background.sub: Another window was in front for the whole session, so all {{span}} were left out and nothing was measured. Keep the game in front to get a reading.

smooth.headline: Smooth session
smooth.sub: Even your worst moments held at {{pct}}% of your average — steady.

dips.headline: Mostly smooth — dips under pressure
dips.sub: High average, but your worst moments ran at {{pct}}% of it. That gap is what stutter feels like.

rough.headline: Rough — frequent stutter
rough.sub: Your worst moments dropped to {{pct}}% of your average — that gap is felt as stutter.

unmeasured.headline: Not graded
unmeasured.sub: A smoothness verdict compares your worst moments with your average, and this session didn't measure both.

sessionDebrief.gpuLoafedInsight: Your GPU only reached {{pct}}% at its peak while frames dipped — so the GPU probably isn't the bottleneck here. Prime suspect: a CPU or system limiter.
sessionDebrief.changesActive: During this session: {{count}} Compy changes active
sessionDebrief.changesActiveUnknown: During this session: Compy changes active — not recorded
sessionDebrief.unknownChangesActive: Compy couldn't read its change history when this session began, or couldn't confirm whether any of its changes were on, so it doesn't know how many of its changes were on. This session can't be the baseline for a test.
sessionDebrief.zeroChangesActive: 0 changes active — you played on stock settings (an honest baseline).
sessionDebrief.replaceComparisonBody: A comparison is already armed ({{title}} · {{game}}). Applying this replaces that baseline with a fresh one.
sessionDebrief.applyFix: Apply the #1 fix — compare next session
sessionDebrief.applyTry: Try one change — compare next session
sessionDebrief.cleanSession: Good session, good rig. Nothing worth changing.
sessionDebrief.comparisonWaitShort: Too short to compare: {{readings}} of the {{min}} readings the {{title}} comparison needs. It's still waiting for your next {{game}} session.
sessionDebrief.comparisonWaitNoReading: No frame reading this session, so the {{title}} comparison is still waiting for your next {{game}} session.

latency.noMouseReports: No mouse reports captured — try again and keep the mouse moving.
latency.diagnosticsUnavailable: Compy couldn't read latency diagnostics just now — this can happen right after launch. Reopen Advanced in a moment to try again.
latency.title: Latency & responsiveness
latency.subtitle: Read-only diagnostics — Compy reports what your machine actually does. Nothing here changes a setting.
latency.msiConfirmed: {{on}} of {{total}} capable devices confirmed on MSI
latency.msiAdvertisedInactive: · {{count}} advertise it but run on a line IRQ
latency.msiUnknown: · {{count}} couldn't be read (not a problem — just not readable)
latency.msiAdvertisesVerified: advertises MSI · verified running on a line IRQ
latency.msiNotAdvertised: no MSI support advertised · on a line IRQ
latency.networkExplainer: How your PC reaches the internet — this shapes online-game latency (ping and lag), separate from the local responsiveness above. Wired Ethernet is the steadiest; Wi-Fi is fine for plenty of games.
latency.timerRangeLabel: Windows can run this timer between {{finest}} (finest) and {{coarsest}} (coarsest) on this machine — {{finest}} is as fine as it goes here.
latency.pollingRateGaming: Gaming-class polling rate (≈1000 Hz or better) — plenty for fast aim.
latency.pollingRateMid: Mid polling rate (≈500 Hz) — fine for most play; gaming mice reach 1000 Hz+.
latency.pollingRateModest: Modest polling rate (≈250 Hz) — usable, but a gaming mouse polls 1000 Hz+.
latency.pollingRateBasic: Basic polling rate (≈125 Hz, office-mouse tier) — a gaming mouse polls 1000 Hz+; the mouse is the limiter here.
